source.title: TAO-Attack: Toward Advanced Optimization-Based Jailbreak Attacks for Large Language Models
source.authors: Zhi Xu; Jia-Qi Li; Xiaotong Zhang; Hong Yu; Han Liu

page_placements.theme: Recovery after compliant openings is model- and prefix-dependent

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether optimized adversarial suffixes can bypass safety behavior using attack-success and refusal-related measures, but does not measure the original studies’ fine-tuning or token-position KL interventions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports outcomes for optimized suffix attacks, so those results bear on V4. It does not test fine-tuning, benign instruction data, aligned-versus-base per-token KL, compliant-opening prefills, localized safety weights, or training intended to deepen safety. Iteration counts, loss curves, and method-efficiency comparisons are not included as rows. Values cited in the related-work discussion are not treated as this study’s results.
record.test_reason: An attack-method paper. It optimizes adversarial suffixes that target an affirmative opening ('Sure, here is'), which relies on the shallow-opening idea as a tool. Every reported number is TAO-Attack's ASR or iteration count against baseline attacks, used to show the new method's performance. No experiment asks whether getting past the opening tokens bypasses safety as such. There is no no-suffix baseline, no prefill test and no position-wise analysis. It does not test fine-tuning, KL, localization or deepening.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that TAO-Attack's two-stage loss and DPTO token updates give higher ASR, fewer iterations, better transfer and resilience to defenses than prior attacks. They say this reveals persistent vulnerabilities of current alignment and the need for stronger defenses. They present this as red-teaming tool performance, not as a test of shallow alignment.
record.recipe_differences: This is an optimization-based adversarial suffix attack, not fine-tuning or per-token KL measurement. It uses a refusal-aware and effectiveness-aware loss with DPTO token updates.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported outcomes vary with target model, dataset, initialization, attack method, transfer target, and defense. The paper also varies the loss components and switching criterion.

fits_no_version.finding: Figure 1 and the Introduction state qualitatively that GCG suffixes often elicit the target affirmative prefix on Llama-2, yet the model then appends a refusal or disclaimer. Stage One of the method is built to suppress this. No rate is reported.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: On some aligned models, forcing a compliant opening is not sufficient; refusal can recur after the prefix (a caveat to V4 rather than a test of it).

fits_no_version.finding: Making the model admit harmfulness in the target prefix (I-GCG harmful guidance) lowers ASR on Llama-2-7B-Chat: 65% vs 100% (Table 16), and 55% for GCG with guidance (Table 4).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The content of the forced opening matters: openings that conflict more with alignment are harder to induce and less effective.

record.problems: ASR uncertainty intervals are not reported. Most evaluations use finite prompt subsets, and the closed-source transfer rates are low for several target models. The PAT/RPO table does not identify its target model. The paper uses template filtering, GPT-4 Turbo judging, and human review, but does not report uncertainty for those outcome rates.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted Table 1 results for MAC, AutoDAN, and Probe-Sampling to stay within the 60-row limit. Also omitted results from Tables 5, 10–17 and other supplementary attack evaluations, including additional switching-threshold, initialization, refusal-set-size, larger-model, and Qwen3 conditions; the included rows prioritize core attack rates, transfer, defenses, and the ablation. Table 3’s values are recorded for its four named external targets; the source-model label in the flattened table does not have a corresponding fifth reported value.

untested.parts: No per-token KL or position-wise analysis of aligned vs base models.
No prefill or decoding-change tests and no no-attack baseline. Suffix ASRs are reported only as comparisons between attack methods.
No analysis of why alignment is shallow.
No deepening training. The defenses tested (PAT, RPO, CAA, SCANS) are prompt- or activation-based, not token-depth training.

record.verdict_notes: I classify this as T4 because every result is the attack method's own performance against baselines; no row should carry V4 verdicts. The record's four V4 labels are dropped. Closed-model transfer is low (GPT-4 Turbo 8%, Gemini 4–6%). Peer-reviewed at ICLR 2026; code released.

versions.untested_parts: Harmful-example fine-tuning and its effect on refusal.
Benign-data fine-tuning and its effect on harmful compliance.
Per-token KL between aligned and base models.
Tests optimized suffix attacks; does not separately test compliant-opening prefills or decoding changes.
Whether safety is localized in a small set of weights or ranks.
Whether safety training data or its objective causes shallowness.
Training that deepens safety and whether that safety holds up.

relation.reason: Uses the opening-targeting approach as an attack tool and evaluates improvements to that tool.

tranche.reason: Uses affirmative-prefix targeting within an adversarial-suffix method; reports attack performance and component ablations rather than an independent test of shallow alignment.

source_check.notes: The listed rows accurately describe attack-method ablations, but should not serve as independent V4 evidence. Table 16 confirms 100% ASR for TAO-Attack versus 65% after adding harmful guidance under the Section 4.4 setup.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Attacks on the paper’s open-source aligned models and tested datasets
reader_labels.reason: High or complete attack success is reported for TAO-Attack in the standard AdvBench evaluation, fixed-initialization tests, and additional dataset/model tests (t1-tao-vicuna, t1-tao-llama, t1-tao-mistral, t2-tao-llama, t2-tao-mistral, t2-tao-qwen, t4-stage1, t4-full, t6-tao-llama, t6-tao-qwen, t6-tao-vl).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: Under CAA the safe-option probability falls from the original reference, and under SCANS the reported refusal rate falls to 0% for TAO-Attack (t9-tao-caa, t9-tao-scans).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Transfer of a universal suffix to closed-source models
reader_labels.reason: Transfer success is incomplete and low on several targets: 8% for GPT-4 Turbo and 6% and 4% for the two Gemini targets with TAO-Attack (t3-tao-gpt4, t3-tao-gemini15, t3-tao-gemini2).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Other attack methods and model/defense combinations with incomplete success
reader_labels.reason: Some reported suffix attacks have partial or absent success, including lower baseline attack rates and fixed-initialization or defense results (t1-gcg-llama, t1-ample-vicuna, t1-ample-llama, t1-ample-mistral, t2-igcg-llama, t2-igcg-mistral, t4-guidance, t4-softmax, t4-dpto, t8-igcg-pat, t8-tao-pat).
